Appendix B • Velocity Units Examples [3.2.3]

B.2 Relative Line-Centered Velocity Units

A second useful observation is that one can define, for each transition \(j\), a line-centered velocity coordinate by choosing the anchor wavelength to be the rest-frame wavelength of that line: \begin{align} v^{(j)} \;\coloneqq\; c\ln\left( \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}}{\lambda_j} \frac{a_\dagger}{a_{\mathrm{obs}}} \right). \tag{B.8} \end{align} Here the superscript \((j)\) indicates that the spectral axis is being constructed using \(\lambda_j\) as the reference wavelength. In other words, this is not a new physical quantity, but simply a different way of labeling the observed spectral axis for the particular line \(j\).

Now consider a photon associated with transition \(j\) that is emitted at \(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{em}}\). Its observed wavelength is \begin{align} \lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}^{j}\left(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{em}}\right) = \lambda_j \frac{a_{\mathrm{obs}}}{a_{\mathrm{em}}}. \tag{B.9} \end{align} Substituting this into the definition of \(v^{(j)}\), we obtain \begin{align} v^{(j)}\left(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{em}}\right) &= c\ln\left( \frac{\lambda_j}{\lambda_j} \frac{a_{\mathrm{obs}}}{a_{\mathrm{em}}} \frac{a_\dagger}{a_{\mathrm{obs}}} \right) = c\ln\left( \frac{a_\dagger}{a_{\mathrm{em}}} \right). \tag{B.10} \end{align} Likewise, if a photon associated with the same transition \(j\) is emitted at \(\vec{x}_f\), then \begin{align} \lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}^{j}\left(\vec{x}_f\right) = \lambda_j \frac{a_{\mathrm{obs}}}{a_f}, \tag{B.11} \end{align} and therefore \begin{align} v^{(j)}\left(\vec{x}_f\right) &= c\ln\left( \frac{\lambda_j}{\lambda_j} \frac{a_{\mathrm{obs}}}{a_f} \frac{a_\dagger}{a_{\mathrm{obs}}} \right) = c\ln\left( \frac{a_\dagger}{a_f} \right). \tag{B.12} \end{align}

The key point is that, once the anchor is chosen as \(\lambda_j\), the dependence on the line wavelength cancels out completely. As a result, the position of a feature in this coordinate depends only on where along the line of sight it was produced, not on which transition is being considered. Therefore, all transitions defined in this way share the same common spectral interval: \begin{align} v^{(j)} \in \left[ c\ln\left(\frac{a_\dagger}{a_f}\right), \; c\ln\left(\frac{a_\dagger}{a_{\mathrm{em}}}\right) \right]. \tag{B.13} \end{align} This is precisely why these coordinates are so useful: after centering each line on its own rest wavelength, all lines span the same velocity-domain range and can be compared on a common axis.

A particularly convenient choice is \(a_\dagger=a_f\). In that case, the lower end of the velocity domain is mapped to zero, and the common interval further simplifies to: \begin{align} v^{(j)} \in \left[ 0, \; c\ln\left(\frac{a_f}{a_{\mathrm{em}}}\right) \right]. \tag{B.14} \end{align}
